title: Hear, O Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4)
hookLine: the Shema is said with a hand over the eyes, attention on one thing
carry: like the four fringes in one hand

cards: The Torah itself says when to say these words: when you lie down, and when you rise up. So they're said every morning and every night, and at bedtime too.

The Talmud tells that Rabbi Akiva, dying, said them, and drew out the last word until his breath ran out. Six Hebrew words. And when the moment comes to say them in the service, something unusual happens.
People don't look up, or at the book. Many raise a hand and cover their eyes, and for a few seconds the world goes dark.

teach.b: In the old Jewish translation, Deuteronomy six reads: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad.
The Hebrew has no word for is, so translators have put this verse into English in more than one way, but the heart of it is clear: one. Start with the first word.
Shema means hear, but in Hebrew it stretches wider: to listen, to understand, to take to heart, even to obey. And it isn't addressed to God.
It's addressed to Israel, to the people: a declaration, said to each other and to yourself. Now the hand.
The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, says that Rabbi Judah the Prince, reaching this verse, would pass his hand over his eyes. The custom of covering the eyes grows from that.
Close off everything you can see, and attend to one thing. The same page praises those who draw out the last word, echad, one, long enough to mean it.
And in a Torah scroll, two letters of this verse are written large: the last letter of shema, an ayin, and the last letter of echad, a dalet. Together they spell ed, witness.
Commentators read that as a hint: whoever says this line stands as a witness.
Hear, in this reading, means more than ears: the whole of the attention, gathered, like the four fringes in one hand.

how: Jews say the Shema in the morning and evening services and at bedtime; for the first verse, many cover their eyes with the right hand and draw out the word echad, and the line is traditionally said at the end of life.

o: notice a sound with your ears alone

games.q: you reach the first line of the Shema in the morning service. what do many people do?
o: cover their eyes with a hand.
games.why: many cover their eyes, as Rabbi Judah the Prince did in the Talmud, to shut out everything else and attend to one thing.

practice: Rest your right hand over your eyes and let the dark settle. If you're Jewish, or you'd like to, say the six words slowly, drawing out the last one: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad.
If not, simply listen in the dark until there's just your breath.

wordCard.voice: Hear. Shema: listen, understand, take to heart. The first word of Judaism's central declaration.

orig.note: Hebrew: hear, listen, understand. the first word of Deuteronomy 6:4.

carryVoice: Your line: like the four fringes in one hand. Hearing, here, takes your whole attention. That's day five hundred sixty-six.
